title: Consonantal i is written j
decision: Write consonantal i as j in all Latin, quotations included: jam, ejus, major, conjungō, Joannēs.
html: The lexicon follows the spelling of the Theodōrus et pater readers, which use the j of Lewis & Short. Between vowels j was pronounced double, so the syllable before it is heavy while its vowel is short (rejice scans heavy although re- is short, Verg. Ecl. 3.96): major, ejus, pejus therefore carry no macron, while long prefixes keep theirs (dējectus, prōjēcit). The letter stays i where it is a vowel: in the interjection iō, in forms of eō (iērunt, adiērunt), in superior, interior, Plēiades, in Iūlus where Vergil makes it three syllables, and after qu and gu (quiēs, reliquiae). Citation labels keep each dictionary’s own headword. Search treats i and j alike.

title: Macrons are spelling
decision: Mark every long vowel, fully and consistently, as part of the spelling.
html: Macrons are treated like the accents of French: part of the word, not an aid for beginners. Short vowels are left plain, and a heavy syllable is not by itself a long vowel. Hidden quantities, long vowels in syllables already heavy by position, are marked too (rēctus, cīnctus).

title: Which authority settles a vowel
decision: Lewis & Short first; Bennett for hidden quantities that Lewis & Short leaves unmarked; de Vaan wherever he explicitly discusses the vowel.
html: Lewis & Short marks most quantities but leaves many hidden ones blank, and Bennett’s study of hidden quantity fills those gaps. De Vaan’s Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008) is the most recent of the three, so where he discusses a vowel he takes precedence (sāriō). Where the authorities conflict, the entry says which one we followed.

title: narrō with a short a
decision: Write narrō, narrāre, not nārrō.
html: De Vaan (s.v. gnārus) derives the verb from *nārāre, shortened by the littera-rule, which Weiss calls the “narro rule”; de Vaan comes first where he discusses a vowel. Bennett’s nārrō rests on a single apex, NÁRREM in the Lyon tablet (CIL XIII 1668), on a syllable already long by position; in those inscriptions only about three apices in four stand on long vowels.

title: frūstrā with a long u
decision: Write frūstrā; frustum, “a piece”, is a different word, with a short u.
html: De Vaan (s.v. fraus) derives it from *fraud-tro-, and Bennett cites an apex (CIL VI 20370): both give a long u.

title: Short vowels before gn
decision: A vowel before gn is short unless its stem is long: magnus, signum, lignum, ignis, dignus, pugnus, pugna, but rēgnum (from rēx), stāgnum, sēgnis, abiēgnus.
html: This follows Bennett, Buck and Allen against the rule reported by Priscian that every vowel before gn is long. It is a deliberate exception to the precedence of de Vaan, whose pūgnus, pūgna (s.v. pungō) are not followed.

title: Perfect subjunctive -erīs, future perfect -eris
decision: The perfect subjunctive has a long ī (nē dīxerīs), the future perfect a short i (sī vēneris). A form that could be either is left short.
html: Bennett, and Allen and Greenough (§169.d), give the perfect subjunctive the long ī of the old optative. A clause drawn into a subjunctive clause counts as subjunctive (cum jūdicāverīs, Ps. 50:6 in Jerome’s psalter from the Hebrew); a general condition with a timeless present, or the polite grātum fēceris, stays short.

title: Clipped -ne keeps an apostrophe
decision: Write satin', vīn', ain', audīn', scīn', vidēn', with the vowel as long or short as in the base word.
html: The apostrophe marks the lost e of -ne. There is no compensatory lengthening: satin' keeps the short a of satis, audīn' the long ī of audīs. A following est keeps its e (satin' est, Ter. Ph. 210).

title: dēbeō is for duty
decision: dēbeō with an infinitive expresses duty or obligation; for what simply had to happen, use necesse est.
html: Lewis & Short: in classical prose it is always used of moral necessity.

title: jentāculum with a short e
decision: Write jentāculum and jentō with a short e.
html: Lewis & Short leaves the e unmarked, and no authority we follow marks it long.

title: linteum and mantēle
decision: The bath towel is linteum and the hand towel mantēle; a tablecloth is also linteum.
html: mantēle is the hand towel in Varro (L. 6.85) and Vergil (A. 1.702), and Martial uses lintea of a tablecloth (villōsa tegant tibi lintea citrum, 14.138). Traupman’s gausapina is classically a frieze coat, and manutergium is found only in Isidore.

title: Turning a tap on and off
decision: On: epitonium vertere. Off: epitonium claudere, or aquam sistere.
html: The verb is Varro’s (epitoniīs versīs, R. 3.5.16); compare Vergil’s sistere aquam fluviīs (A. 4.489). Traupman’s versāre and reversāre are not used: reversāre is late Latin. In narration, forms that do not sound the same in present and perfect are preferred (epitoniō versō, not vertit).

title: furcilla for the fork
decision: The table fork is furcilla, not fuscinula.
html: furcilla is a classical word (Varro, Cicero) whose table-fork sense is modern (Traupman 71). fuscinula occurs only in the Vulgate.

title: opus caementīcium for concrete
decision: Concrete is opus caementīcium, not Traupman’s concrētum.
html: After Vitruvius’s caementīcius.

title: exedra for the sitting room
decision: The sitting room is exedra, not sessōrium.
html: exedra is a room for sitting and conversation in Vitruvius and Cicero (Traupman 125). The ancient senses of sessōrium are “seat” and, in one passage of Petronius, “dwelling”.

title: gelātum for ice cream
decision: Ice cream is gelātum; Traupman’s congelidum crēmum and Morgan–Owens’s glaciēs dulcis are given as alternatives.
html: Antiquity had no ice cream to name, so the choice is between modern coinages. This one is the easiest to say, and it has modern precedent (Helfer; Vox Latina, both cited by the Neo-Latin Lexicon).

title: cedo with short vowels
decision: Cedo! “give it here” has a short e and a short final o, and its plural is cette.
html: Lewis & Short marks it cĕdo and lists it apart from cēdō, cēdere “go, give way”. It is an old imperative, from -ce and the root of dō.

title: lutra with a short u
decision: Write lutra, not Lewis & Short’s lūtra.
html: Lewis & Short gives no evidence for the long vowel, and its only etymological note, luō, has a short one. De Vaan (2008: 355) prints lutra and Proto-Italic *udrā-, from PIE *ud-ro- “of the water”, with the short u of Sanskrit udrá- and Greek ὕδρος. The long vowel of Lithuanian ūdra and Russian vydra comes from a Balto-Slavic lengthening (Winter’s law), which says nothing about Latin. Italian and Portuguese lontra and French loutre continue a short u; a long ū would have given u, as in luna and lune. The word occurs only in prose (Varro, Pliny), so verse cannot decide.

history.html: Cites Russian vydra, as de Vaan does, in place of a Bulgarian form: the lexicon is English–Latin.

title: fortasse with a short final e
decision: Write fortasse, not Lewis & Short’s fortassē.
html: Lewis & Short gives no evidence for the long vowel. De Vaan (2008: 236, s.v. fors) speaks of the word’s “short final vowel”, and verse proves it: in Catullus 85.1, Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam fortasse requīris, the fifth foot, -tasse re-, must be a dactyl, so the e is short. Horace scans it the same way (S. 1.3.20, 1.6.98).

title: caccabus: a short a and a double c
decision: Write caccabus (also cacabus), not Lewis & Short’s cācabus.
html: The word is Greek κάκκαβος, with a short α and a double κ. Varro writes caccabum (cited by Lewis & Short), and Statius scans albōrum calicum atque caccabōrum (Silv. 4.9.45) with a heavy first syllable, which the double c explains. Lewis & Short’s cācabus marks that heavy syllable as a long vowel. Our Comenius quotation table still follows Lewis & Short.

title: mixtus with a short i
decision: Write mixtus, mixtōria, permixta without a macron on the i.
html: Traupman marks the i long, but Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked in mixtum, and de Vaan (2008: 382–383) prints mixtum, mixtūra with a short i, explaining mixtum as syncopated from *mixitum. Spanish mestizo and French métis, from Late Latin mixtīcius, also continue a short i. Bennett has not been checked yet.

title: oiei keeps its i
decision: Write oiei as Lewis & Short prints it, not ojei.
html: It is unclear whether the i’s of this interjection are vowels or consonants, so the j rule is not applied. The form also depends on the edition: the Perseus text of Terence does not print oiei at the places Lewis & Short cites. For a plain “ouch”, au is the better-attested word.

title: ōlla with a long o
decision: Write ōlla, ōllae with a long o.
html: ōlla is the later form of aula (Festus: aulās antīquī dīcēbant, quās nōs dīcimus ōllās), and an o that comes from au is long, as in cōda beside cauda and plōstrum beside plaustrum. Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked; the quantity is hidden by the double l.
